Consistent Is Not Correct

Four papers from this year’s AIME-Con look at using large language models to build Q-matrices, estimate item difficulty, and write the reasons behind a score. After reading all four, I have become more careful. A consistent result easily makes us believe it is also correct.
I Nyoman Indhi Wiradika
Published October 10, 2026
12 min read

In early October 2026, the National Council on Measurement in Education (NCME) held its second AI in Measurement and Education Conference (AIME-Con) in Pittsburgh. NCME is the professional association in the United States for people who design and study tests. Through AIME-Con, its members discuss the use of artificial intelligence in building, scoring, and interpreting assessments. The conference papers are openly available on the ACL Anthology; links to the four papers I discuss are in the references.

All four papers test the output of large language models (LLMs) that is then used in measurement. That is where my attention goes as someone who studies test construction. Before counting the time or money that could be saved, I want to know whether the output is fit to use.

A Q-matrix maps the skills needed to answer each question. That mapping shapes our conclusions about which skills a student has mastered. If an LLM builds it wrongly, our conclusions about students can be wrong too. So I need to check a Q-matrix made by an LLM, just as I would check one put together by experts.

Stable, Agreed, and Valid
Before turning to each paper, I want to separate three things that I sometimes mix up myself.

If I run the same procedure again and get the same result, I call it stable. If several models or several runs give the same answer, there is agreement. Then how do I know the result is fit for my measurement purpose? For that I need a reference outside the model, such as an expert Q-matrix, calibrated item parameters, or a human rater’s reasoning. Agreement with that reference is part of the validity evidence I need to check.
A result that is stable and shared by many models is convincing. But neither is enough to show that the result is valid.

All four papers
My own summary of the four papers. A procedure needs the first two checks to be usable at all, but only the third tells me whether it measures what I intended.
1. Same Model, Same Prompt, Different Students
Kim (2026) · AIME-Con Full Papers, pp. 649–655Read the paper ↗

If I could choose only one paper for my students to read, I would choose Kim’s. A Q-matrix states which skills each item requires, and in cognitive diagnosis it decides how a student’s answers turn into a mastery profile. To make this easier to picture, think of the Q-matrix as a list of the skills needed to answer each question. For example, item 7 needs fractions and reading a graph, while item 8 needs only fractions. If the list is wrong, the diagnosis is wrong, however good the statistics are. Building that list takes time and often starts arguments, so it is understandable that several recent studies ask an LLM to draft it from the item text. Most of them report the result of a single run, or a majority vote across several runs.

Minkwon Kim (Teachers College, Columbia) used the 23 released TIMSS 2011 grade-8 mathematics items, a published seven-attribute expert Q-matrix, and real responses from 741 U.S. students. Three open-weight models (Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3-medium) each regenerated the full matrix ten times with sampling and ten times with greedy decoding.

These two terms are worth understanding first. With sampling, the model chooses among several possible next words, so two runs can differ. The amount of variation depends on the temperature setting. A lower value makes the model lean toward the most likely word, while a higher value gives other choices more room. This setting affects how much the answers vary; it does not guarantee they are right. With greedy decoding, the model always takes the single most likely word, so every run should be the same. Each matrix was then fitted with the DINA model, and the resulting student classifications were compared.

Kim (2026), Tables 1–2 and Section 4.4. A profile counts as changed if any of the seven attributes changes. Greedy decoding removes run-to-run variation, but most profiles still differ from those produced by the expert Q-matrix.

Two sampled runs of the same model, with the same prompt and the same temperature, gave different mastery profiles to 61% to 88% of students. The students were the same. So were their responses. Greedy decoding made every run identical down to the byte, which shows the instability came from sampling. That stable result still differed from the result based on the expert Q-matrix: 63% to 76% of students’ mastery profiles changed when the two matrices were compared.

The section on majority voting made me pause longer. The idea is to pick, for each cell of the matrix, the mapping that appears most often. It is a common way to deal with results that change from run to run, and the voted matrix was almost identical, cell by cell, to the greedy one. Yet differences in just a few cells changed the diagnosis for half of the students or more. How similar the two matrices looked hid a large difference in what students would actually receive.

Kim also points out that the comparison reference has its limits. The expert Q-matrix is not ground truth. Earlier statistical validations also show that some skill mappings in the expert Q-matrix need another look. Model disagreement was indeed somewhat higher on those contested items (0.847 versus 0.659 per item), although the permutation test did not reach conventional significance (p = .060). This finding gives repeated runs another use: items whose skill mapping keeps changing can be flagged for expert review.
2. Seven Models Agreed, Mostly With Each Other
Chrzan & Domingue (2026) · AIME-Con Works in Progress, pp. 24–36Read the paper ↗

The title of this paper, Consensus without accuracy, names the problem directly. Asking an LLM for an absolute difficulty score has a weak track record, so Michael Chrzan (University of Maryland) and Benjamin Domingue (Stanford) asked the models to compare two items and decide which one is harder.

To picture it, imagine we want to order a few objects from lightest to heaviest without knowing their exact weights. We compare two objects at a time and decide which is heavier. After enough comparisons, we can put them in order. In this study, the LLM does something similar: it compares two test items and picks the harder one.

Seven frontier models from OpenAI and Google compared items from seven datasets in the Item Response Warehouse, 179 items in all, each with difficulties already calibrated from real responses. A hierarchical Bayesian Bradley–Terry model pooled the judgments and estimated how sharply each model discriminated and how much it favoured whichever item came first.

Looking only at the internal measures, the models’ results seem convincing. Most showed triplet transitivity above 95%. That means when a model judged item A harder than B, and B harder than C, it usually also judged A harder than C. The order makes sense. Agreement among the seven models was also high in every dataset (Krippendorff’s α from 0.834 to 0.917). But when the pooled ranking was compared with IRT difficulty computed from test-takers’ responses, the match was only moderate (Spearman ρ = 0.400 overall), ranging from 0.250 to 0.591 across datasets.

I picture five raters with the same training sitting in one room. They can agree with each other and still miss what makes a question hard for a fifteen-year-old in a classroom. According to the authors, models can do the same. They may agree on prominent features of the text, the curriculum topic, or the number of solution steps, while missing what actually trips up respondents. Adding a sixth rater with a similar view may make the ranking look more settled, while the source of the error stays the same.

How each model judges also matters. Discrimination varied widely across models, and several showed a position bias large enough for the 94% interval to exclude zero. The authors suggest using LLM rankings as a provisional order when reviewing items or drafting an early version of a test. For final calibration parameters, this evidence is not yet enough. I agree with that limit.
3. Anchors Help, but Only So Far
Bezirhan & von Davier (2026) · AIME-Con Full Papers, pp. 365–371Read the paper ↗

Of the four papers, this approach gave me the most hope. Its results also reminded me not to stop at a single correlation. Ummugul Bezirhan and Matthias von Davier (TIMSS & PIRLS International Study Center, Boston College) used anchor items that were already calibrated to judge new items. They compared each new item with those anchors and fixed the anchors’ difficulty in the Bradley–Terry model. Earlier we only put objects in order by weight; now we have a few objects whose weight we already know. Those objects become the reference for estimating the weight of a new one. Anchor items work the same way. Their difficulty is already known, so new items can be placed on the same scale.

The anchors were 80 TIMSS grade-4 mathematics trend items, and the targets were 101 new TIMSS 2023 items whose operational difficulties were held back for validation. A small open model (Qwen3-8B, deterministic decoding) played three judges with different prompts and made 11,607 pairwise judgments. Across all 101 items, the estimates correlated with operational difficulty at r = .484. Had I only read that number, I might have called the correlation moderate and moved on. The authors looked further.

Inside the anchor range the correlation was r = .372. For items below that range, the method captured practically no difference in difficulty. The overall .484 came partly from the distance between the two groups, not from precision within each group. The authors conclude that the method can interpolate but not extrapolate, and that the design of the comparison network may matter as much as the choice of judge. Back to the weights. We have references for estimating objects whose weight falls between the ones we compare against. If a new object turns out lighter or heavier than every reference we have, the estimate becomes less reliable. The study shows a similar limit. The items I worry about most in a new item bank are often the very easy and the very hard ones, and those can fall outside the available anchor range.

Two other details are worth noting. The model reported a confidence of 0.85 in nearly every comparison, so its confidence carried no information. And its labels of “slight” or “moderate” difference followed its own certainty, not the real difficulty gap (r = −.02).
4. Similar Words, Different Judgments
Jung, Lu, Darici & Brüegge (2026) · AIME-Con Full Papers, pp. 466–471Read the paper ↗
This paper is the closest to my work as a teacher. In formative assessment, students read the reason behind a score as feedback. In this paper, that reason is called a rationale.

Several studies compare LLM and human rationales using embedding-based cosine similarity. The term is technical, but the basic idea is easy to follow. Each text is turned into a long list of numbers, and the method measures how closely the two lists point in the same direction. Texts with similar topics and word choices get a high score. Julie Jung and colleagues (Harvard Graduate School of Education, with clinical partners in Germany) checked whether that similarity score can show that an LLM’s rationale contains the main point made by the human rater. That point is what a student needs to receive as feedback.

The study used data from a clinical reasoning assessment of 21 medical students who took part in AI-simulated patient encounters. Ratings came from one human rater and 27 configurations of ChatGPT-5.4 (model size, reasoning effort, and prompt type), producing 5,790 rationale pairs. Each pair was then labelled fully aligned, partially aligned, or not aligned by a calibrated coding pipeline, and the partially aligned category was split into three subtypes.

Jung et al. (2026), Section 5 and Table 3; the axis is truncated to show differences. After adjustment, fully and partially aligned pairs did not differ (p = .576), and none of the three subtypes differed from each other. Rationales that missed the human rater’s main point received the highest mean similarity.

Similarity could only screen out pairs that were clearly misaligned, nothing more. It could not tell full from partial alignment. Within the partially aligned category, rationales that missed the human’s main point scored as high as rationales that kept it. Imagine a student reading feedback that sounds like the teacher’s comment but leaves out exactly the point they need to fix. Similar wording does little for that student.

The similarity score was also affected by text length. The LLM’s rationale was longer in 89% of pairs, and larger length gaps lowered similarity regardless of meaning. Rationales written in German scored about 0.12 lower than those in English. That difference made me curious about how Indonesian would fare. The authors themselves acknowledge that their codes are not ground truth. Their conclusion is limited to what this similarity measure can do. I agree that similarity alone is not enough to show that an LLM’s rationale can replace a human’s.

After reading these four papers, I understand better why LLM results need a closer look. The answer can stay the same every time, be shared by other models, or sound like a human judgment. All of that makes it easy to believe. Even a fairly good overall correlation can lead us to overlook a group of items that is actually estimated poorly.

So before using the results, I want to know how they compare with student response data or expert judgment. This kind of check is already routine when we build tests. When using AI, I feel I still need to do it, even when the first results look convincing.
Five Things I Want to Ask When LLMs Are Used in Research
When reviewing manuscripts or supervising student projects, I see LLMs being used more and more often. These four papers helped me sharpen what I need to ask before accepting the results.

Which model was used, and how was it set up?I want to know the model and its version, and settings such as temperature, top-p, top-k, and seed. These details help others repeat the study in the same way. In Kim’s study, for example, the top-k actually in use followed the model’s own default of 20, not the library default of 50 that readers usually assume. Small details like this are easy to miss.

If you run it again, does the result change?I want to see results from several runs and how much the classifications or parameters change. A single result does not show that. A majority-vote result should also come with information about the variation that existed before the runs were combined.

Is the result only consistent, or has it been compared with response data?Transitivity shows whether the model’s ordering makes sense. Agreement between models shows whether they give the same answer. Both need to be kept apart from the match with test-takers’ response data. If only consistency and agreement were checked, I still want to see evidence that the result is fit for that measurement purpose.

What difficulty range do the anchor items cover?Anchors help place new items on a difficulty scale that is already known. I want to know whether the new items still fall within that range. If they turn out easier or harder than every anchor, the limits of the estimate need to be explained.

What is used to check the LLM’s results?For me, test-takers’ response data and human judgment should remain the reference. An LLM can help flag items that need review or put together an early ordering of an item bank. But before item parameters are used to interpret scores, I still want to see field-test results and expert review.
What About Using LLMs in Indonesia?

If you have ever built an item bank or a diagnostic test in Indonesia, this situation may feel familiar. Many items need to be prepared, pretest data is still scarce, and expert time is limited. In those conditions, I understand why LLMs are tempting to try.

I would use them myself to help find questions whose skill mapping is still unclear. An LLM can also help build a provisional difficulty order, as long as the anchor items cover the range needed. For the reasons behind a score, I can use it to draft, then check whether the main point a student needs to receive is there. The results still need to be compared with an expert Q-matrix, field-test data, or human judgment, depending on how they are used.

But what happens when the questions and the feedback are in Indonesian? All four studies used English items, or English and German rationales. We cannot simply assume the results will be the same in Indonesian. I would like to see these approaches tested with questions and responses from test-takers here. It feels like research we could start ourselves.
Consistent is a good start. But consistent is not necessarily correct.
